6:["$","div",null,{"className":"lg:col-span-8","children":[["$","header",null,{"className":"mb-12","children":[["$","h1",null,{"className":"font-serif font-light text-5xl md:text-6xl text-navy mb-4 leading-tight","children":"Squire \"Squirre\" Rolle"}],["$","div",null,{"className":"w-24 h-[2px] bg-gold"}]]}],["$","section",null,{"className":"prose prose-navy max-w-none","children":[["$","div",null,{"className":"relative mb-12","children":[["$","$L3",null,{"iconNode":[["path",{"d":"M16 3a2 2 0 0 0-2 2v6a2 2 0 0 0 2 2 1 1 0 0 1 1 1v1a2 2 0 0 1-2 2 1 1 0 0 0-1 1v2a1 1 0 0 0 1 1 6 6 0 0 0 6-6V5a2 2 0 0 0-2-2z","key":"rib7q0"}],["path",{"d":"M5 3a2 2 0 0 0-2 2v6a2 2 0 0 0 2 2 1 1 0 0 1 1 1v1a2 2 0 0 1-2 2 1 1 0 0 0-1 1v2a1 1 0 0 0 1 1 6 6 0 0 0 6-6V5a2 2 0 0 0-2-2z","key":"1ymkrd"}]],"className":"lucide-quote absolute -left-8 -top-8 h-16 w-16 text-gold/10 pointer-events-none"}],["$","h2",null,{"className":"font-serif font-bold text-3xl text-navy mb-6","children":"Biography"}],["$","div",null,{"className":"text-navy/80 text-xl leading-relaxed prose prose-navy max-w-none  prose-headings:font-serif prose-headings:font-bold prose-headings:text-navy  prose-h3:text-3xl prose-h3:mt-10 prose-h3:mb-4 prose-a:text-gold hover:prose-a:text-navy prose-a:transition-colors prose-img:rounded-md prose-img:shadow-md prose-img:mx-auto prose-img:border prose-img:border-gold/20 prose-blockquote:border-l-4 prose-blockquote:border-gold prose-blockquote:pl-8  prose-blockquote:italic prose-blockquote:text-navy/80 prose-blockquote:font-serif prose-blockquote:text-2xl prose-blockquote:ml-8 prose-blockquote:my-10 [&_blockquote_p::before]:hidden [&_blockquote_p::after]:hidden","children":[["$","h3","h3-0",{"children":"The Biography of Squire \"Squirre\" Rolle"}],"\n",["$","p","p-0",{"children":"Squire \"Squirre\" Rolle stands as a profound and emblematic figure of the Exuma islands in The Bahamas. While detailed, individualized written records of his life remain sparse—a systemic reality for the enslaved and formerly enslaved people of the Caribbean whose histories were often ignored or erased by colonial administrators—his story is deeply entwined with the massive Rolle plantations, the famous slave uprisings of the early 19th century, and the eventual creation of the Exumian commonage system. To understand Squire Rolle is to understand the sweeping saga of survival, resistance, and legacy that defines the people of Great Exuma. His life is a testament to the thousands of African descendants who transformed a name given by oppressors into a badge of unyielding community and kinship."}],"\n",["$","h4","h4-0",{"children":"The Roots of the Rolle Legacy in Exuma"}],"\n",["$","p","p-1",{"children":"The story of Squire Rolle begins not with his birth, but with the complex geopolitical shifts of the late 18th century. Following the American Revolutionary War, thousands of British Loyalists fled the newly independent United States, seeking refuge in other parts of the British Empire. Many of these Loyalists, bringing with them enslaved Africans, settled in The Bahamas. Among the most prominent of the land grantees was Denys Rolle, a wealthy English aristocrat and Loyalist from Florida, who was granted thousands of acres of land on Great Exuma by the British Crown. Denys Rolle, and later his son, Lord John Rolle, established a series of sprawling cotton plantations across the island."}],"\n",["$","p","p-2",{"children":"The conditions on these plantations were incredibly harsh. Enslaved individuals were forced to clear the rocky, unforgiving Bahamian soil to plant cotton, a crop that rapidly depleted the land's nutrients. The blistering heat, the constant threat of disease, and the brutal discipline enforced by the overseers made life on the Exuma plantations a daily struggle for survival. Squire Rolle would have been born into or lived through this intense period of enslavement, his daily life dictated by the punishing rhythms of agricultural labor under the scorching Caribbean sun."}],"\n","$Lb","\n","$Lc","\n","$Ld","\n","$Le","\n","$Lf","\n","$L10","\n","$L11","\n","$L12","\n","$L13","\n","$L14","\n","$L15","\n","$L16","\n","$L17","\n","$L18","\n","$L19","\n","$L1a","\n","$L1b","\n","$L1c","\n","$L1d","\n","$L1e","\n","$L1f"]}]]}],"$L20","$L21",false]}],"$L22"]}]
7:["$","script","script-0",{"src":"/_next/static/chunks/2uyb8-0enc77-.js","async":true}]
8:["$","script","script-1",{"src":"/_next/static/chunks/2z-jpqdx1wamk.js","async":true}]
9:["$","script","script-2",{"src":"/_next/static/chunks/26bq-cr7az8tz.js","async":true}]
a:["$","$L23",null,{"children":["$","$24",null,{"name":"Next.MetadataOutlet","children":"$@25"}]}]
b:["$","p","p-3",{"children":"The enslaved people on these estates were treated entirely as property, stripped of their ancestral names and forced to adopt the surname of their enslaver: Rolle."}]
c:["$","blockquote","blockquote-0",{"children":["\n",["$","p","p-0",{"children":"\"In the crucible of the plantation, a name intended to signify ownership was forged by the enslaved into an unbreakable bond of collective identity and shared survival.\""}],"\n"]}]
d:["$","p","p-4",{"children":"For Squire Rolle, bearing the name \"Rolle\" was a daily reminder of his bondage. Yet, over time, as the enslaved community grew and formed deep familial and social networks, the name began to take on a new meaning. It became a marker of belonging among the enslaved population of Exuma. Squire Rolle, like many others, found ways to maintain his humanity. In the shadows of the plantation houses, under the cover of night, the enslaved Rolles passed down oral traditions, practiced traditional African spirituality and bush medicine, and created tight-knit communities that the plantation owners could never fully control."}]
e:["$","h4","h4-1",{"children":"The Pompey Rebellion and the Spirit of Resistance"}]
f:["$","p","p-5",{"children":"The defining moment of the Rolle plantation era—and a period that would have profoundly shaped Squire Rolle's life—was the famous slave rebellion of 1829. By the late 1820s, the cotton industry in Exuma was failing. The shallow, rocky soil was exhausted, pests like the chenille bug decimated crops, and profits were plummeting. In a bid to maximize his remaining assets, Lord John Rolle decided to transfer a group of his enslaved laborers from Exuma to Cat Island, another Bahamian island where he hoped they could be put to more profitable use."}]
10:["$","p","p-6",{"children":"This decision sparked outrage and terror among the enslaved community. For people like Squire Rolle, Exuma was the only home they knew. Their families, their communities, their secret gardens, and the graves of their ancestors were all intimately tied to that specific land. They refused to be uprooted, separated, and treated as mere cargo."}]
11:["$","p","p-7",{"children":["Led by a courageous enslaved man named ",["$","$L26","a-0",{"slug":"pompey","href":"/profiles/pompey","children":"Pompey"}],", a group of enslaved individuals actively rebelled against the transfer. They laid down their tools, retreated into the dense bush, and eventually, Pompey and a small group stole a boat and sailed to Nassau, the capital of The Bahamas, to petition the Governor against their forced relocation. Though Pompey was brutally flogged for his insubordination, the rebellion was ultimately successful. The Governor intervened, recognizing the potential for widespread unrest, and the forced transfer to Cat Island was halted."]}]
12:["$","p","p-8",{"children":["$","img","img-0",{"src":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d4/Exuma_in_the_Bahamas.svg/800px-Exuma_in_the_Bahamas.svg.png","alt":"A historical map of The Bahamas, highlighting the Exuma cays where the Rolle plantations were situated."}]}]
13:["$","p","p-9",{"children":["While ",["$","$L26","a-0",{"slug":"pompey","href":"/profiles/pompey","children":"Pompey"}]," is remembered as the heroic face of this resistance, he did not act alone. The rebellion was supported by the entire enslaved community, including figures like Squire \"Squirre\" Rolle, who stood firm in their defiance. Squire's role in this era represents the everyday, collective resistance of the Exumian people—those who refused to work, those who provided food and shelter to the rebels, and those who collectively declared that their connection to the land was stronger than the chains of their bondage. Their collective resilience laid the crucial groundwork for the unique status they would soon achieve."]}]
14:["$","h4","h4-2",{"children":"Emancipation and the Creation of the Commonage"}]
15:["$","p","p-10",{"children":"The long, arduous struggle for freedom culminated in the passing of the Slavery Abolition Act in 1833, which officially came into effect in The Bahamas on August 1, 1834. This was followed by a controversial and difficult period of \"apprenticeship,\" designed to ease the transition for the slave owners, which finally ended in 1838. When true, unmitigated freedom finally arrived, the formerly enslaved people of Exuma faced a daunting new reality. They were legally free, but they possessed virtually nothing in terms of capital or resources."}]
16:["$","p","p-11",{"children":"However, the story of Exuma took a unique and historic turn. Lord John Rolle, perhaps driven by a combination of complex factors—including the realization that the land was no longer agriculturally viable for large-scale farming, the undeniable strength of the Exumian people's connection to the land, and perhaps a measure of practical concession—made an unprecedented decision. He deeded all of his vast landholdings in Exuma, encompassing thousands of acres and entire settlements like Rolleville, Rolle Town, Mount Thompson, and Steventon, to his former slaves and their descendants in perpetuity."}]
17:["$","p","p-12",{"children":"This extraordinary act created the \"commonage\" system, a form of communal land ownership that remains legally binding and culturally fundamental today. Under this system, the land cannot be bought, sold, or alienated to outsiders; it is held in trust for anyone who can prove direct descent from the original enslaved Rolles."}]
18:["$","p","p-13",{"children":"For Squire Rolle, this transition from an enslaved laborer to a free landowner was monumental. He and his peers were now the undisputed masters of their own destiny. They transitioned from forced, backbreaking cotton cultivation to independent subsistence farming, fishing, and self-governance. They built their own homes on their own land, established their own independent churches, and created a deeply self-reliant, resilient society. Squire Rolle would have been a respected elder or a vital community leader during this crucial period of grassroots nation-building. He helped to establish the unwritten rules, agricultural practices, and communal traditions that governed the newly freed settlements, ensuring that the land would sustain them for generations."}]
19:["$","h4","h4-3",{"children":"The Cultural Legacy and the Rolle Surname Today"}]
1a:["$","p","p-14",{"children":"The legacy of Squire \"Squirre\" Rolle and his generation is vividly and powerfully alive in modern-day Exuma and throughout the broader diaspora of The Bahamas. Today, \"Rolle\" is arguably the most common surname in the country, a direct, living legacy of the thousands of enslaved people who inherited both the name and the land."}]
1b:["$","blockquote","blockquote-1",{"children":["\n",["$","p","p-0",{"children":"\"We are not just a name; we are a nation within a nation. The blood of the ancestors runs deep in this rocky soil, and the land belongs to us as surely as we belong to the land.\""}],"\n"]}]
1c:["$","p","p-15",{"children":"The commonage lands of Exuma remain a fiercely protected heritage. Over the decades, foreign developers and investors have frequently attempted to purchase these prime coastal lands, envisioning luxury resorts and private estates. However, the descendants of Squire Rolle and his contemporaries have successfully and repeatedly defended their ancestral birthright, fighting in courts and in the public square to uphold Lord Rolle's original deed. The settlements of Rolleville and Rolle Town are living monuments to this history—communities where the concept of family extends to the entire village, and where the past is palpably present in the layout of the streets, the ruins of the old plantation structures, and the stories told by the elders."}]
1d:["$","p","p-16",{"children":["Squire \"Squirre\" Rolle may not have lengthy, detailed entries in the colonial archives, but his life is indelibly inscribed in the very landscape of ",["$","a","a-0",{"href":"/islands/exuma","target":"_blank","rel":"noopener noreferrer","children":"Exuma"}],". He embodies the arduous journey from trauma to triumph, from considered property to proud proprietor. As a figure of historical memory, he serves as a powerful reminder that the true builders of the Caribbean were not the colonial lords who claimed the land from afar, but the enslaved and formerly enslaved men and women who cultivated it with their sweat, fought for it with their blood, and ultimately claimed it as their enduring home. His story is a vital, beating thread in the vibrant tapestry of Bahamian history, a narrative of enduring strength that continues to inspire new generations of Bahamians to protect their heritage and their land."]}]
1e:["$","h3","h3-1",{"children":"References"}]
